strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely problem: existing video MLLMs often perform deceptively well on multiple-choice QA with random distractors, but fail under realistic, visually and semantically confusing alternatives in action recognition.
Using domain-specialized SOTA action recognition models (TIM, AVION) to mine hard adversarial distractors for both evaluation and training is an effective and scalable contribution.
The authors provide an insightful analysis into the language interface: showing how compressed/lemmatized official class keys harm LLM semantic interpretation compared to natural narrations.

The paper includes systematic ablation studies (both incremental addition in Table 3 and leave-one-out in Table 7) that demonstrate the individual contributions of vision token supervision, temporal boundary detection, direct prediction, and memory.
Strong empirical results on the proposed EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA benchmark and notable improvements over strong baselines like LLaVA-Video-7B and GPT-4o.
weaknesses: When evaluated on the standard EPIC-KITCHENS-100 classification setting (Table 4), the model acts essentially as a re-ranker over the top-20 predictions of TIM. While it achieves 58.3% vs TIM's 56.4% (+1.9%), this improvement comes at the cost of deploying a 7B MLLM requiring substantial training (32 GH200 GPUs) and inference compute.

The gains across broader external video benchmarks (Table 5) are relatively minor (+0.4% on LongVideoBench, +0.6% on VideoMME, -0.4% on NextQA), suggesting limited out-of-domain transfer outside egocentric / kitchen environments.

The memory/context mechanism relies on ground truth previous actions during training and its own previous predictions during test-time augmentation, which could be prone to error propagation in long, unsegmented real-world action sequences.

Several presentation and proofreading oversights remain (e.g., unfinished URL placeholder in the abstract 'available at:', typos such as 'Snice MVBench' in Section 13, and grammatical quirks in figure callouts).

strengths: Compelling benchmark formulation: Using state-of-the-art specialized action models (e.g., TIM, AVION) to mine hard distractors effectively exposes the visual shortcomings of leading MLLMs (including GPT-4o) that are typically masked by random or trivial distractors.

Comprehensive and well-structured ablations: The manuscript provides both additive (Table 3) and leave-one-out (Table 7) ablation studies, clearly detailing the relative impact of egocentric prompting, hard distractor supervision, visual token supervision, temporal detection, and prior action context.

Solid empirical results on the target task: Fine-tuning LLaVA-Video with the proposed framework leads to substantial improvements on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, notably outperforming zero-shot GPT-4o by over 20 points.

Insightful analysis of dataset representations: The comparison between official compressed verb-noun keys versus natural language narrations in EPIC-KITCHENS provides useful guidance for training language-centric multimodal models on video tasks.

Generalization across broader video understanding benchmarks: The model demonstrates consistent, non-trivial improvements over baseline LLaVA-Video on external action-centric benchmarks such as MVBench, EgoSchema, and PerceptionTest.
weaknesses: Comparison setup on standard EPIC-KITCHENS-100: In Table 4, LLaVAction evaluates by re-ranking the top-20 candidate predictions produced by TIM, rather than performing standard classification from scratch over the entire label space. While practical, this makes direct comparison to standard end-to-end models (such as standalone TIM or AVION) somewhat uneven, and this caveat should be made prominent in the main text and abstract.

Benchmark bias towards the distractor generator: The proposed EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA benchmark relies on TIM's top confidences to define distractors. Although the authors mitigate training leakage by training on AVION-mined distractors (OOD setting), the evaluation distribution remains inherently tied to the specific inductive biases and failure modes of TIM.

Incremental algorithmic novelty: Several individual components (e.g., timestamp regression, direct prediction, prompt framing, GPT-4o caption distillation) are engineering combinations of known vision-language tuning practices rather than fundamentally new architectural paradigms.

Mixed transfer to general video benchmarks: Improvements on general video benchmarks in Table 5 are modest (e.g., +0.6 on VideoMME, +0.4 on LongVideoBench, and a slight regression of -0.4 on NextQA), showing that while action recognition improves, broader multi-modal reasoning capabilities see limited transfer.

strengths: Principled Hard-Distractor Formulation: The paper correctly identifies that standard random distractor generation in video MQA renders benchmarks overly trivial and uninformative for assessing MLLMs on fine-grained human activity. Mining distractors from state-of-the-art specialized action models (e.g., TIM, AVION) is a simple, scalable, and effective way to evaluate and supervise MLLMs on fine-grained actions.

Comprehensive and Effective Training Pipeline: The proposed components—intermediate vision token supervision, temporal boundary detection auxiliary loss, egocentric prompt framing, and prior action context—are well motivated and show cumulative performance gains on the MQA action benchmark.

Thorough Experimental Validation and Ablations: The empirical study is detailed, featuring systematic leave-one-out ablations (Table 7) and step-by-step additions (Table 3), as well as evaluations on both open-vocabulary narrations and official EPIC-KITCHENS-100 keys.

Insightful Linguistic Analysis: The discussion highlighting why compressed 'official keys' (verb-noun pairs) can introduce grammatical ambiguity and mislead text-sensitive LLM backbones compared to natural language narrations provides valuable insight for video-language modeling.
weaknesses: Re-ranking Formulation Rather than Direct Full-Vocabulary Classification: In the standard EPIC-KITCHENS-100 benchmark (Table 4), LLaVAction functions as a second-stage reranker over the top-20 predictions generated by TIM, rather than performing end-to-end action classification across the full label space. While the authors explicitly acknowledge this, it limits the claim of direct state-of-the-art action recognition compared to standalone models.

Modest Generalization to Broader Benchmarks: On general video-LLM benchmarks (Table 5), the improvements over the LLaVA-Video-7B baseline are relatively small (+0.4% to +2.5%, with a slight regression of -0.4% on NextQA), suggesting that the action-specific training has limited transfer beyond fine-grained physical action scenarios.

Potential Evaluation Leakage / Distribution Shift: Even in the out-of-distribution (OOD) setting where AVION is used for training distractors and TIM for testing, both distractor models were trained on the exact same video corpus (EPIC-KITCHENS-100), meaning candidate choices share strong latent feature correlations.

High Annotation and Compute Overhead: The multi-task pipeline introduces over 530K auxiliary QA and caption pairs generated via GPT-4o distillation, alongside significant GPU requirements (GH200 clusters), which somewhat complicates isolating the exact algorithmic gains versus data scaling effects.

strengths: Addresses an important and relevant problem: evaluating and improving fine-grained, contrastive action understanding in video Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), where standard benchmarks often rely on easily distinguishable random distractors.

The proposed hard example mining using specialist action recognition models (e.g., TIM, AVION) provides a practical and automated way to construct challenging multiple-choice action questions without human annotation or reliance on closed-source LLMs.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets and tasks, including the proposed EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, four traditional action recognition datasets (EPIC-KITCHENS-100, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen-30, MECCANO, Animal Kingdom), and 13 general video MLLM benchmarks.

Extensive ablations and analyses, including leave-one-out and additive ablations, token architecture variations, computational efficiency comparisons with multi-round appending, and attention-based interpretability analysis.
weaknesses: Dependency on specialist models for structured action recognition: The reported State-of-the-Art results on standard action recognition benchmarks (e.g., EPIC-KITCHENS-100, Table 4) rely on a two-stage pipeline where the top-K candidates (K=20) are first filtered by an existing specialist model (TIM). Consequently, LLaVAction functions as a candidate re-ranker whose performance is bounded by the specialist's top-K recall, making the comparison to standalone end-to-end models somewhat asymmetrical.

Limited conceptual novelty: The individual core components—mining hard distractors via classification logits, adding an auxiliary supervised token (analogous to a CLS token or prompt token with cross-entropy loss), and two-stage retrieve-and-rerank inference—are well-established techniques in machine learning and vision-language modeling.

Marginal transfer to general video benchmarks: While LLaVAction shows large improvements on in-domain fine-grained action tasks, the gains over the LLaVA-Video-7B baseline across the 13 general video benchmarks (Table 7) are mostly modest (e.g., +0.1 on EgoSchema, +0.6 on VideoMME w/o subtitles, -0.4 on NextQA), indicating limited broader generalization of the acquired temporal reasoning.

Potential distractor bias in benchmark curation: Distractors generated from a specific specialist model (TIM or AVION) inherently reflect the specific confusion matrix and inductive biases of that architecture, which may introduce domain- or model-specific evaluation artifacts.

strengths: Sound and effective benchmark motivation: Using state-of-the-art specialist action recognition models (e.g., TIM, AVION) to mine hard distractors is an elegant, scalable, and automated approach that exposes real limitations in MLLMs' fine-grained action understanding without relying on costly human annotations or LLM generation.

Comprehensive multi-perspective training curriculum: Combining adversarial distractors, temporal boundary detection (timestamp prediction), prior action conditioning, and open-ended captioning provides a well-rounded recipe for adapting MLLMs to complex video action tasks.

Practical two-stage structured action prediction: The proposed re-ranking paradigm neatly bridges the gap between open-ended generative MLLMs and traditional closed-set action recognition benchmarks with thousands of fine-grained classes, achieving massive computational speedups (190x) over full label vocabulary scoring.

Broad evaluation across diverse domains: Experiments demonstrate applicability beyond egocentric cooking (EPIC-KITCHENS, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen), extending to industrial assembly (MECCANO) and fine-grained animal behavior (Animal Kingdom), alongside evaluation across 13 general video MLLM benchmarks.

Thorough ablation and analytical studies: The paper includes meaningful additive and leave-one-out ablations, action token design exploration, attention correlation analysis, and psychometric difficulty curve analysis.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on specialist models for structured action prediction: In the standard action recognition benchmarks (EPIC-KITCHENS, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen, Animal Kingdom), LLaVAction functions primarily as a second-stage re-ranker conditioned on top-K predictions from strong specialist backbones (TIM, VideoMAE). The paper should explicitly report the oracle top-K recall of the first-stage models to clarify the theoretical upper bound and isolate how much gain comes from re-ranking vs. visual understanding.

Performance gains in Table 2 are largely driven by in-domain supervised finetuning: The large gap over zero-shot models (e.g., GPT-4o, base LLaVA-Video) on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA is primarily a consequence of supervised training on 530K samples from the EPIC-KITCHENS training set. While the distinction between AVION (OOD) and TIM (IID) distractors is appreciated, the visual distribution and domain remain in-domain.

Limited transfer to general video benchmarks: On the 13 general video understanding benchmarks (Table 7), the improvements over the baseline LLaVA-Video-7B are modest (mostly within 0.5%–2%, with minor drops on tasks like VideoDC and NextQA), indicating that while catastrophic forgetting is mitigated via data replay, the fine-grained action tuning provides limited positive transfer to broad video-language tasks.

Marginal contribution of the action token: In the leave-one-out ablation (Table 11), removing the action token only degrades accuracy from 74.1% to 73.6% (a 0.5% difference), whereas data reformulation components (like adversarial distractors) account for the vast majority of the performance gains.

strengths: Insightful benchmarking approach: Generating multiple-choice distractors using specialized action recognition models (e.g., TIM, AVION) exposes significant blind spots in existing leading MLLMs (such as GPT-4o and LLaVA-Video), demonstrating that random distractors mask deficiencies in fine-grained action comprehension.

Comprehensive data reformulation recipe: The combination of adversarial distractor training, temporal boundary detection, sequential prior-action context, and captioning provides a well-rounded strategy to equip MLLMs with temporal and fine-grained visual-action priors.

Well-motivated action token design: Introducing a learnable action token supervised via auxiliary verb, noun, and action classification losses encourages the MLLM to retain action-critical visual representations throughout transformer layers, supported by attention and ablation analyses.

Extensive empirical validation: The framework demonstrates consistent gains across varied domains—egocentric kitchen tasks (EPIC-KITCHENS-100, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen-30), assembly (Meccano), and animal behavior (Animal Kingdom)—as well as across 13 general video MLLM benchmarks.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on specialist models for structured prediction: The two-stage structured action prediction relies on an external specialist (e.g., TIM, VideoMAE) to provide top-K candidate proposals during inference. Consequently, the MLLM functions primarily as a re-ranker, and its performance is upper-bounded by the candidate recall of the first-stage specialist.

Confounding comparisons with zero-shot closed-source models: The paper highlights a 21-point improvement over GPT-4o on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA; however, LLaVAction is fine-tuned on over 500K samples derived from the EPIC-KITCHENS training set, whereas GPT-4o is evaluated strictly zero-shot. While the authors use out-of-distribution (AVION) distractors, in-domain dataset exposure remains a strong confounding factor.

Marginal improvements on general video benchmarks: On broader video benchmarks (Table 7), the performance improvements over the baseline LLaVA-Video-7B are modest (e.g., +0.1 on TempCompass, +0.4 on VideoEval-Pro, and slight regressions on NextQA and VideoChatGPT), indicating that gains are predominantly localized to fine-grained action discrimination rather than translating broadly across general video reasoning.
